title: Tasting like a sommelier
lead: The Court's Deductive Tasting Method: look, smell, taste, then reason to a conclusion, and what climate and age look like in the glass.

court.outcome: Evaluate and describe 20 classic wines of the world. Understand the Deductive Tasting Method to build vocabulary and skills for objective evaluation and description of classic wines and major grape varieties. Recognize and explain climatic and winemaking effects on wine style.

coverage.topic: Exam content: how wines and grape varieties look, smell and taste
coverage.guide: Know how classic grapes and wines tasted in class look, smell and taste; no tasting on the exam.

coverage.topic: Learning objective: evaluate and describe 20 classic wines
coverage.guide: Describe 20 classic wines; the journal gives each one a page.
Fault check, then fruit and non-fruit words for whites and reds.
Color intensity, primary color, tearing; staining on reds.
Sound or faulty; delicate to powerful; youthful, developing or vinous.

coverage.topic: Journal: Nose - fruit and fruit condition
coverage.guide: Name the category and fruit; condition from tart to liqueur.

coverage.topic: Journal: Nose - non-fruit, new oak, earth, mineral
coverage.guide: Grape/vineyard vs. winemaking notes; yes or no for oak, earth, mineral.
Recheck fruit and non-fruit; note any change from the nose.
Sweetness, acidity, alcohol, body; bitterness on whites, tannin on reds.
Link the wine to grape, climate, country, region, quality level, vintage.

coverage.topic: Learning objective: climatic and winemaking effects on style
coverage.guide: Read climate from fruit, acidity and alcohol; winemaking from non-fruit notes.
coverage.where: Climate and age in the glass; Nose: non-fruit clues

coverage.topic: Journal: Introduction to Deductive Tasting (initial and final conclusion)
coverage.guide: Initial then final conclusion, each backed by reasons; ages 1-3 to 10+.
Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Chenin Blanc: climates, regions, styles, structure, color.
Eight reds, Pinot Noir to Tempranillo: climates, regions, styles, structure, color.

intro.title: THE FOUR STEPS
intro.text: Describe first, conclude last. Every conclusion needs a reason you wrote down earlier.

sections.name: How the Court tastes

lines.label: At Level 1
lines.text: The course introduces the Deductive Tasting Method. You will not be asked to taste on the exam. You will be asked how classic wines and grapes look, smell and taste.

lines.label: At Level 2
lines.text: The Certified exam is four wines in 45 minutes on a written grid. Every line on the grid scores a point.

know: Introductory exam: no tasting, no service performance, no vintage memorizing.
Questions focus on wines tasted in class.
The Certified grid has five parts: color, fruit, non-fruit, structure, conclusion.
Advanced and Master use a longer format: sight, nose, palate structure, palate, initial and final conclusion.
Level 1 uses a Tasting Journal with pages for 20 classic wines.

visuals.text: The Certified tasting: two whites and two reds, about 11 minutes each.

sections.name: Sight

lines.label: What to check
lines.text: Clarity, depth of color, main color, any second color, and the rim on reds. Then tears (legs) and any bubbles.

lines.label: What it hints
lines.text: Whites deepen toward yellow and brown with age. Reds fade and turn more see-through. Thick legs hint at more alcohol or sugar.

know: White main colors on the Certified grid: straw, yellow, gold.
Red main colors: purple, ruby, garnet.
Rim variation and staining are checked on reds only.
Nebbiolo and Grenache can show an orange or garnet rim even young.
Level 1 journal: intensity pale, medium or deep; tearing light, medium or heavy.

items.label: WHITE
items.title: Straw · Yellow · Gold
items.text:
Deepens with age
Moves toward yellow, then brown

items.label: RED
items.title: Purple · Ruby · Garnet
items.text:
Fades with age
More transparent over time

sections.name: Nose: fruit

lines.label: Big to small
lines.text: Name the fruit family first, then one specific fruit. Then say what state the fruit is in: tart, ripe, jammy, dried and so on.

lines.label: Where aromas come from
lines.text: Primary aromas come from the grape. Secondary come from winemaking. Tertiary come from aging.

know: White fruit groups on the grid: apple/pear, citrus, stone fruit, tropical.
Red fruit groups: red, black, blue.
Pick one or two fruit-condition words for nose and palate.
If a fruit group is absent, mark 'No' and write 'None'.
First ask: is the wine in good condition? Corked (TCA) smells of wet cardboard.

items.name: Primary
items.text: From the grape: fruit, herbs, flowers

items.name: Tertiary
items.text: From aging: vanilla, nuts, savory notes

visuals.title: Fruit words in the Level 1 lexicon

rows.name: Tropical
rows.meta: pineapple, mango, passion fruit, banana, lychee

rows.name: Black fruit
rows.meta: blackberry, black cherry, black plum, black currant

visuals.note: The first four are white-wine groups; the last three are red.

sections.name: Nose: non-fruit clues

lines.label: The rule
lines.text: Each non-fruit line is Yes or No. Say Yes only when it is a key part of the wine. Leave nothing blank.

lines.label: Winemaking shows
lines.text: Many lines point straight to a winemaking choice. Learn the marker words for each.

know: Butter, cream, yogurt = malolactic fermentation.
Dough, bread, yeast, cheese rind = lees.
Vanilla, toast, smoke = new oak; on reds also coconut and dill.
Ginger, honey, saffron, wax = noble rot.
Earth = wet leaves, forest floor, mushroom; mineral = wet stone, sulfur, saline.

visuals.title: Marker words on the white grid

rows.name: Lees
rows.meta: dough, baked bread, yeast, cheese rind

visuals.note: From the Court's Certified white grid (1-2025).

sections.name: Palate and structure

lines.label: Confirm
lines.text: On the palate, check the fruit and non-fruit you found on the nose. Has anything changed?

lines.label: Structure
lines.text: Then judge sweetness, acidity, alcohol, body, and tannin on reds or bitterness on whites. The Court says to trust structure.

know: White grid sweetness choices: dry or off-dry.
Phenolic bitterness is a white-wine line; tannin is a red-wine line.
Tannin is the drying, sandpaper feel on the tongue.
Finish length runs short to long; complexity runs simple to high.
Level 1 journal: sweetness dry, off-dry or sweet; body light, medium or full.

visuals.title: Sweetness, driest to sweetest
visuals.note: Advanced and Master format; the Certified white grid uses Dry or Off-Dry.

sections.name: Wine information review

lines.label: What it is
lines.text: After describing a wine, the Level 1 journal asks you to connect it to theory. You list five things that make the wine unique.

lines.label: What you fill in
lines.text: Grape, climate, country, region and appellation, official quality level where one exists, and vintage.

know: List the wine's five most distinctive aromas and flavors.
Pick one climate: cool, moderate or warm, using acidity and alcohol.
Name the countries and regions that classically grow the grape.
Give a quality level only where the law has one, like Rioja Reserva.

visuals.title: Quality levels the journal lists
visuals.note: Only where the law has quality levels.

sections.name: Climate and age in the glass

lines.label: Climate
lines.text: Read climate from fruit condition and structure. Tart fruit and high acid point cool. Riper fruit, lower acid and more alcohol point warm.

lines.label: Age
lines.text: Read age from fruit condition, color, fruit versus savory notes, and sediment. Fresh fruit turns dried as wine develops.

know: Warmer grapes make more sugar, so wines carry more alcohol.
Cool-climate reds: higher acidity, lower alcohol, lighter body.
Cool-climate whites: higher acidity, citrus, green orchard fruit.
Age words on the nose: youthful, developing, vinous.
The Level 1 journal ties climate to structure: look at acidity and alcohol.

items.label: COOL
items.title: Tension
items.text:
Tart fruit
Higher acidity
Lower alcohol
Lighter body

items.label: WARM
items.title: Ripeness
items.text:
Riper fruit
Lower acidity
Higher alcohol
Fuller texture

sections.name: Conclusions

lines.label: Certified
lines.text: Pick the grape from six listed, then climate, country and an age range. Give reasons from your notes. Finish with a short sales pitch.

lines.label: Advanced and Master
lines.text: An initial conclusion narrows the options. The final names grape, country, region, appellation, quality level, style and vintage.

know: Climate choices: cool, moderate, warm.
White age ranges: 1-2, 3-4, 5+ years. Red: 1-3, 4-6, 7+ years.
Every conclusion needs specific reasons from your description.
Check your notes match your answer: off-dry plus Sauvignon Blanc is a warning sign.
Level 1's intro to deductive tasting uses ages 1-3, 3-5, 5-10 and 10+ years.

items.name: Climate
items.text: Cool, moderate or warm, with reasons

sections.name: Grape profiles: whites

lines.label: The profiles
lines.text: The Court’s Grape Variety Profiles show each grape’s climates, top regions, styles, structure and color. Four of them are white.

lines.label: Region names
lines.text: Some regions imply the grape: Sancerre means Sauvignon Blanc, Vouvray means Chenin Blanc.

know: Chardonnay: Burgundy, Champagne (Blanc de Blancs), California, Oregon, Victoria.
Sauvignon Blanc: Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé, Bordeaux, Marlborough; Fumé Blanc in California.
Riesling: high acidity, dry to sweet; Germany, Alsace, Clare Valley.
Chenin Blanc: Vouvray and Savennières in the Loire; Steen in South Africa.

visuals.title: Four whites and their classic homes
visuals.note: From the Court’s Grape Variety Profiles.

sections.name: Grape profiles: reds

lines.label: Eight reds
lines.text: The profiles cover Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Grenache, Nebbiolo, Sangiovese and Tempranillo.

lines.label: Climate
lines.text: Pinot Noir grows cool to warm. Grenache, Sangiovese and Tempranillo are marked warm to hot. Nebbiolo is marked high for both tannin and acidity.

know: Pinot Noir: Burgundy, California, Oregon, New Zealand; whole cluster is an option.
Syrah is Shiraz in Australia; Northern Rhône: Hermitage, Côte-Rôtie, Saint-Joseph.
Grenache is Garnacha Tinta or Garnatxa in Spain.
Nebbiolo is Barolo and Barbaresco, and Chiavennasca in Valtellina.
Tempranillo: Rioja, Ribera del Duero (Tinta del País), Toro (Tinta de Toro).

visuals.title: Eight reds and their classic homes
visuals.note: From the Court’s Grape Variety Profiles.

mixups.why: Lees smell like bread, dough or cheese rind; malolactic smells like butter, cream or yogurt.
Fruit is what you smell (lemon, cherry); condition is its state (tart, ripe, jammy, dried).
Bitterness is scored on whites; tannin is scored on reds.
Certified has five boxes and asks country; the longer format adds region, appellation, quality level and vintage.

facts.fact: Introductory learning objective: understand the Deductive Tasting Method to build vocabulary and skills for objective evaluation and description of classic wines and major grape varieties.
Introductory learning objectives also include evaluating and describing 20 classic wines and recognizing climatic and winemaking effects on wine style.
Section 2 of the Introductory course is 'CMS Wine Evaluation Technique'. The Introduction to the Deductive Tasting Method in Section 12 is marked 'Not tested at this level'.
Introductory exam content includes how wines and grape varieties look, smell and taste, focusing on wines tasted in class. Wine tasting itself is not tested.
A student will not be tested on wine tasting, performance of service elements or vintage memorization.
Certified tasting exam: four wines (two whites, two reds) identified in 45 minutes using the CMS-A Deductive Tasting Method; about 11 minutes per wine.
Certified white grid (CMS-A 1-2025) sections: COLOR, FRUIT, NON-FRUIT, STRUCTURE, CONCLUSION, then 'Sell this wine to a guest in two sentences or less.' Every line must be answered.
White grid primary color choices: Straw, Yellow, Gold. Red grid: Purple, Ruby, Garnet.
White grid fruit lines: Apple/Pear, Citrus, Stone Fruit, Tropical (Yes/No, name one specific fruit or write 'None'). Red grid fruit lines: Red, Black, Blue.
Fruit condition choices (nose and palate): Tart, Ripe, Overripe, Jammy, Candied, Baked, Dried, Bruised. Select one or two.
Non-fruit descriptors combine nose and palate. Select 'Yes' only if it is an important character of the wine; select 'No' if not; answer every line.

White non-fruit lines include: Flowers; Fresh Herbs, Hay; Green Bell Pepper, Grass, Jalapeño, Asparagus; Grape Variety Spice; Noble Rot/Botrytis: Ginger, Honey, Saffron, Wax; Oxidation: Nuts, Dried Fruit; Lees: Dough, Baked Bread, Yeast, Beer, Cheese Rind; Malolactic Fermentation: Butter, Cream, Yogurt; Petrol, Gasoline, Rubber; Earth: Wet Leaves, Mushroom, Compost; Mineral: Mineral, Wet Rock, Sulfur; New Oak: Vanilla, Toast, Smoke, Cinnamon, Nutmeg, Clove.

Red non-fruit lines include: Flowers; Fresh Herbs, Tomato Leaf; Dried Herbs; Green Bell Pepper etc.; Mint, Eucalyptus; Black Peppercorn; Coffee, Cocoa, Mocha; Meat, Blood, Leather; Balsamic, Tar; Carbonic Maceration; Earth: Forest Floor, Wet Leaves, Mushrooms, Compost; Mineral; New Oak: Vanilla, Smoke, Toast, Coconut, Dill.
White structure: Phenolic Bitterness (Yes/No), Sweetness (Dry/Off-Dry), Acidity and Alcohol (Low to Medium-, Medium, Medium+, High). Red structure: Tannin, Acidity, Alcohol on the same scale.
Conclusion: primary grape variety (from examinable varieties), climate (Cool, Moderate, Warm), country of origin, age range. White age: 1-2, 3-4, 5+ years. Red age: 1-3, 4-6, 7+ years.
Advanced and Master format (2024) sections: SIGHT, NOSE, PALATE STRUCTURE, PALATE, INITIAL CONCLUSION, FINAL CONCLUSION.

Sight: clarity (clear, hazy, cloudy); intensity (translucent to opaque); primary color (white: water white, straw, yellow, gold; red: purple, ruby, garnet); secondary colors; rim variation and staining (reds only); tearing; gas evidence.

Nose: minor faults (e.g. barnyard, nail polish remover, struck match); aromatic intensity (delicate to powerful); age assessment (youthful, developing, vinous); fruit; fruit condition; non-fruit from grape and from winemaking; earth; mineral; oak (new oak yes/no, intensity, descriptors, type: French, American, Eastern European).

Palate structure: sweetness (bone dry, dry, dry with slight residual sugar, off-dry, medium-sweet, sweet, lusciously sweet), acidity, alcohol, body, phenolic bitterness (whites), tannin volume and texture (reds), texture.
Palate: confirm fruit, fruit condition, non-fruit, earth, mineral and oak from the nose; then balance, length of finish (short to long) and complexity.

Initial conclusion: possible grapes, climate (cool, moderate, warm), possible countries, age range (1-3, 3-5, 5-10, 10+ years). Final conclusion: grape or blend, country, region and appellation, official quality level, official style category, vintage.

For every conclusion, give specific reasons from your description. Climate: look at fruit condition and structure (acidity, alcohol). Age: look at fruit condition, color, fruit vs savory focus, and sediment.
Prep advice: 'Why is it from a particular climate? Look at the fruit condition and structure.' World of origin: look at fruit, fruit condition, earth and mineral.
Answer 'Yes' only if very apparent and key to the wine's identity. You must tick 'No' to earn the point; 'Look at structure and trust structure'.
Six grape varieties are listed to choose from on the actual Certified exam, and the list changes by exam; candidates must name the country of origin.
Review before choosing: if you called the wine off-dry and chose Sauvignon Blanc, look back for where things went off-track. Use theory on growing and winemaking to make informed choices.
Four steps of tasting: look, smell, taste, think/conclude.

Primary aromas come from the grape (fruit, herbs, flowers); secondary from winemaking, mostly yeast (and yogurt or sour cream from malolactic); tertiary from aging (e.g. vanilla from oak, nutty notes); tertiary aromas often turn fresh fruit more dried and concentrated as a wine develops.
As white wines age they become more yellow and brown; red wines lose color and become more transparent.
Nebbiolo and Grenache often show a garnet or orange rim even when young; Malbec often has a magenta rim.
Thicker, more viscous legs suggest more alcohol or residual sugar.
Tannin is the drying, sandpaper-like feel on the tongue in red wines; higher-alcohol, riper wines usually have more texture.
Warm climates generally give riper fruit and less acidity; cool climates give tart fruit and more acidity.

Cool-climate reds tend to have higher acidity, lower alcohol, lighter body and more savory or spicy aromas; cool-climate whites have higher acidity with citrus, green orchard fruit, flowers and mineral freshness.
Warmer-climate grapes build higher sugar, giving higher-alcohol wines; cooler-climate grapes keep more acidity.

The Court's Introductory Sommelier Course 'Wine Evaluation Technique' Tasting Journal (CMS-A 2024) has pages for Wine #1 to Wine #20, then an 'Introduction to Deductive Tasting' part with pages for two wines.
Course learning objective: 'Evaluate and describe 20 classic wines of the world.'
Journal lexicon: Presence of fault: corked wine, TCA (trichloroanisole): cardboard, wet paper, chlorine, mildew.

Journal lexicon, white fruit: apple/pear (green, red, yellow); citrus, tart (lemon, lime, grapefruit) and sweet (orange); stone fruit (peach, nectarine, apricot); tropical (pineapple, mango, passion fruit, banana, lychee). Red fruit: red (cherry, raspberry, cranberry, strawberry, pomegranate); black (blackberry, black cherry, black plum, black currant); blue (blueberry).

Journal lexicon, white non-fruit from the grape or grape growing: flowers; fresh herbs; green bell pepper, jalapeño, grass, asparagus; grape variety spice; botrytis/noble rot (ginger, saffron, honey, wax); petrol (gasoline, rubber). From winemaking: lees contact (dough, baked bread, yeast, beer, cheese rind); malolactic (butter, cream, yogurt); oxidation (nuts, dried fruit); new oak (vanilla, toast, smoke, cinnamon, nutmeg, clove, caramel).

Journal lexicon, red non-fruit from the grape or grape growing: flowers (lilac, violet, lavender, rose, potpourri); fresh herbs; green bell pepper; dried herbs; black peppercorn; coffee, cocoa, mocha; raw meat, cured meat, leather. From winemaking: vinegar, nail polish, barnyard; carbonic maceration (bubble gum, red fruit candy, banana, stemmy); oxidation; new oak (adds coconut and dill on reds). Earth: wet leaves, forest floor, mushrooms, compost. Mineral: mineral, wet stone, sulfur, saline.

Journal sight: intensity of color (pale, medium, deep); primary color (white: straw, yellow, gold; red: purple, ruby, garnet); tearing (light, medium, heavy); staining yes or no, red wines only. Nose: is the wine in good condition (yes or no); aromatic intensity (delicate, medium, powerful); age assessment (youthful, developing, vinous); fruit category and description; fruit condition (tart, ripe, overripe; fresh, baked, dried, stewed, bruised; juicy, jammy, candied, liqueur); non-fruit from the grape or grape growing and from winemaking; new oak, earth, mineral each yes or no.

Journal palate: for all categories, are there differences from the nose to the palate? Structure: sweetness (dry, off-dry, sweet); acidity and alcohol (low to medium minus, medium, medium plus, high); body (light, medium, full); phenolic bitterness yes or no, white wines only; tannin (low to medium minus to high), red wines only.

Journal Wine Information Review: grape variety (or dominant grape); list five of the wine's unique aromas and flavors; climate cool, moderate or warm, using structure such as acidity and alcohol; which countries, regions and appellations classically grow the grape; official quality level where appropriate (Burgundy: Village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru; Beaujolais: Village, Cru; Alsace: Village, Grand Cru; Rioja: Reserva, Gran Reserva; Chianti: Classico, Riserva; Germany: Kabinett, Spätlese); vintage; and the wine tasted.

Journal Introduction to Deductive Tasting: initial conclusion (possible grapes, climate cool/moderate/warm, possible countries, age range 1-3, 3-5, 5-10 or 10+ years), each with specific reasons from the description; then final conclusion (grape, country of origin, region and appellation, official quality level, vintage).

Grape Variety Profiles (CMS-A, courtesy of GuildSomm) help new students learn grape names, where grapes grow, regions and growing conditions, winemaking, and typical aromas, flavors and structure. Marks: * = region that implies the grape; ** = grape synonym.

Chardonnay profile: still and sparkling; climates cool, moderate, warm; dry; styles tart, decadent, oaked, unoaked, fruity; possible winemaking: lees contact, malolactic fermentation, new oak; top regions Burgundy*, Champagne* (Blanc de Blancs**), California, Oregon, Victoria (Australia); color straw, lemon, gold.

Sauvignon Blanc profile: dry and sweet; climates cool, moderate; styles unoaked, oaked, tart, juicy, savory; possible winemaking: lees contact, new oak; body bar light to medium; acidity bar toward high; top regions Loire (Sancerre*, Pouilly-Fumé*), Bordeaux (Sauternes*), Marlborough (New Zealand), Casablanca (Chile), California (Fumé Blanc**); color lemon to gold.

Riesling profile: dry, sweet and sparkling; climates cool, moderate; sweetness bar dry to sweet; body bar light to medium; acidity at high; styles tart, juicy, sweet, fruity, unoaked; top regions Southwest Germany, Alsace (France), Clare Valley (Australia); color pale straw to deep gold.

Chenin Blanc profile: dry, sweet and sparkling; climates cool, moderate, warm; sweetness bar dry to sweet; acidity bar toward high; styles tart, textural, sweet, decadent, unoaked; possible winemaking: lees contact, malolactic; top regions Loire (Bonnezeaux*, Quarts de Chaume*, Vouvray*, Savennières*) and South Africa (Steen**); color lemon to gold.

Pinot Noir profile: Burgundy bottle and glass; climates cool, moderate, warm; styles fruity, tart, juicy, savory, textural; possible winemaking: whole cluster, neutral oak, new oak; top regions Burgundy*, California, Oregon, New Zealand; color pale ruby to deep ruby.

Cabernet Sauvignon profile: Bordeaux bottle and glass; climates moderate, warm, hot; styles fruity, oaked, tannic, savory, decadent; possible winemaking: destemming, blending, new oak; top regions Bordeaux*, California, Washington, Chile, Australia; color deep ruby, ruby, purple, dark purple.

Merlot profile: Bordeaux bottle and glass; climates moderate, warm; styles fruity, oaked, ripe, textural, decadent; possible winemaking: destemming, blending, new oak; top regions Bordeaux*, California, Chile; color medium ruby, deep ruby, purple.

Syrah profile: Burgundy bottle, Bordeaux glass; climates moderate, warm, hot; styles spicy, tart, juicy, savory, textural; possible winemaking: blending, large barrel, whole cluster; top regions Northern Rhône (Hermitage*, Côte-Rôtie*, Saint-Joseph*) and Barossa, Australia (Shiraz**); color deep ruby to deep purple/violet.

Grenache profile: Burgundy bottle and glass; climates warm, hot; styles fruity, unoaked, ripe, spicy, decadent; possible winemaking: large barrel, blending, whole cluster; top regions Southern Rhône, Spain (Garnacha Tinta**, Garnatxa**), Australia; color medium to deep ruby.

Nebbiolo profile: Burgundy bottle and glass; climates moderate, warm; tannin and acidity both marked at high; styles tart, textural, tannic, savory, juicy; possible winemaking: large barrel, extended skin maceration; top regions Piedmont (Barolo*, Barbaresco*) and Lombardy (Valtellina*, Chiavennasca**); color medium ruby, deep ruby, garnet.

Sangiovese profile: Bordeaux bottle and glass; climates warm, hot; styles oaked, tart, juicy, savory, tannic; possible winemaking: large barrel, neutral oak, blending; top region Tuscany (Chianti*, Brunello di Montalcino**); color pale ruby, deep ruby, garnet.

Tempranillo profile: Bordeaux or Burgundy bottle, Burgundy glass; climates warm, hot; styles fruity, tart, ripe, savory, oaked; possible winemaking: blending, large barrel, neutral oak, new oak; top regions Rioja*, Ribera del Duero* (Tinta del País**), Toro* (printed 'Tinto del Toro'); color moderate ruby, deep ruby, garnet.
Certified column, Castilla y León: Tempranillo synonyms Tinta del País and Tinta de Toro.

unverified: Partly resolved Nov 2, 2026: the Introductory Tasting Journal (2024) was fetched and is now used. The Introductory Workbook is still not public, and the Curriculum Guide has no tasting subject, so the outcome above quotes the Course Guide's learning objectives.

Wine Folly says the Court stopped using 'Old World' and 'New World' in blind tasting. The current Court grids ask for country of origin and have no Old/New World line, but no Court announcement was fetched to confirm the change.
The Certified exam guide's prep page still says 'Why is it from a particular world of origin?' while the grid asks for country; wording may lag behind the grid.
Color and leg hints (aging color changes, rim colors by grape, legs and alcohol) come from Wine Folly, not the Court.
The cool-vs-warm compare block's 'fuller texture' for warm wines rests on Wine Folly's note that riper, higher-alcohol wines have more texture.

Structure words for the grape profiles (e.g. 'acidity toward high', 'light to medium body') are read off unlabeled bars in the Court's Grape Variety Profiles; only Nebbiolo's tannin and acidity, and Riesling's acidity, sit clearly at 'High'.
The Toro profile prints 'Tinto del Toro'; this chapter uses 'Tinta de Toro', the spelling in the Court's Curriculum Guide (Certified column).

read.bigIdea: Describe the wine first, then reason to an answer.
read.where: The Court teaches the **Deductive Tasting Method**. At Level 1 it builds the words and skills to describe classic wines and major grapes. You won’t taste on the exam, but you will be asked how classic wines **look, smell and taste**. In class you fill in the Court’s **Tasting Journal**, which has pages for **20 classic wines**.

stops.name: Sight
stops.text: Check **clarity**, color and, on reds, the **rim**.

stops.name: Nose
stops.text: Fruit first, then non-fruit, earth, mineral and oak.

stops.name: Palate
stops.text: Confirm what you smelled, then judge **structure**: sweetness, acidity, alcohol and tannin.

stops.name: Conclusion
stops.text: Name the grape, climate, country and age. Back each one with a reason from your notes.

read.bigIdea: Color gives you the first clues about a wine.
read.where: Check **clarity**, how deep the color is, and the main color. On reds, look at the **rim**. Then check the **tears** (legs) and any bubbles.

stops.name: The Level 1 journal
stops.text: Note color **intensity** (pale, medium or deep), the **primary color**, and **tearing** (light, medium or heavy). On reds, also mark **staining**: yes or no.

stops.name: White wine
stops.text: As white wines age, they turn more **yellow** and then **brown**.

stops.name: Red wine
stops.text: As red wines age, they lose color and turn more **transparent**. **Nebbiolo** and **Grenache** often show a garnet or orange rim even when young.

stops.name: Legs
stops.text: Thicker, more viscous **legs** suggest more **alcohol** or **residual sugar**.

keyPoints.line: then name one specific fruit.
groups: apple/pear, citrus, stone fruit, tropical.
groups: red, black and blue.

read.bigIdea: Name the fruit, then describe its condition.
read.where: Work from big to small. Name the fruit family first, then one specific fruit. If a family isn’t there, mark **No** and write **None**.

stops.name: Condition and intensity
stops.text: First, is the wine sound? A **corked** wine (**TCA**) smells like cardboard, wet paper, chlorine or mildew. Then rate **aromatic intensity** (delicate, medium or powerful) and age (**youthful**, **developing** or **vinous**).

stops.name: White wines
stops.text: **Apple/pear**, **citrus**, **stone fruit** and **tropical**.

stops.name: Red wines
stops.text: **Red**, **black** and **blue** fruit.

stops.name: Fruit condition
stops.text: Say what state the fruit is in: **tart**, **ripe**, **overripe**, **jammy**, **candied**, **baked**, **dried** or **bruised**. The Level 1 journal adds **fresh**, **stewed**, **juicy** and **liqueur**.

read.mixup: **Fruit** is what you smell, like lemon or cherry. **Fruit condition** is its state: tart, ripe, jammy or dried.

or cream points to malolactic fermentation.
or dough points to lees.
or toast points to new oak.

read.bigIdea: Non-fruit smells often show how a wine was made.
read.where: Every non-fruit line on the grid gets a **Yes** or **No**. Say Yes only when it’s a key part of the wine, and never leave a line blank. You must tick No to earn the point. The Level 1 lexicon sorts non-fruit notes in two: from the **grape or vineyard**, and from **winemaking**.

stops.name: Malolactic
stops.text: **Butter**, **cream** and **yogurt** point to **malolactic fermentation**.

stops.name: Lees
stops.text: **Dough**, **baked bread**, **yeast** and **cheese rind** point to **lees**.

stops.name: New oak
stops.text: **Vanilla**, **toast** and **smoke** point to **new oak**. On the red grid, oak also covers **coconut** and **dill**.

stops.name: Noble rot
stops.text: **Ginger**, **honey**, **saffron** and **wax** point to **botrytis** (noble rot).

stops.name: Earth and mineral
stops.text: **Earth** means wet leaves, forest floor, mushrooms or compost. **Mineral** means wet stone, sulfur or saline. On reds, **bubble gum** and **red fruit candy** point to **carbonic maceration**.

read.visualIntro: The full list from the white grid:
read.mixup: **Lees** smell like bread, dough or cheese rind. **Malolactic** smells like butter, cream or yogurt.

keyPoints.line: the fruit and non-fruit you found on the nose.
is sweetness, acidity, alcohol, body and tannin.
is the drying, sandpaper feel in red wine.
is scored on whites; tannin is scored on reds.
is the Court’s own advice.

read.bigIdea: The palate checks the nose, then measures structure.
read.where: First, confirm the fruit and non-fruit you found on the nose. Then judge the **structure**: sweetness, acidity, alcohol and body, plus **tannin** on reds or **phenolic bitterness** on whites. The Court’s advice: **trust structure**. The Level 1 journal asks the same thing: is anything **different from the nose**?

stops.name: Sweetness
stops.text: The Certified white grid asks **Dry** or **Off-Dry**. The longer Advanced format runs from **bone dry** to **lusciously sweet**. The Level 1 journal uses **Dry**, **Off-Dry** or **Sweet**, and body is **light**, **medium** or **full**.

stops.name: Acidity and alcohol
stops.text: Both are scored **Low to Medium-**, **Medium**, **Medium+** or **High**.

stops.name: Tannin
stops.text: **Tannin** is the drying, sandpaper-like feel on your tongue in red wine. Whites get **phenolic bitterness** instead.

stops.name: Finish
stops.text: Last, judge balance, how long the **finish** lasts, and **complexity**.

read.visualIntro: The full sweetness scale, driest to sweetest:
read.mixup: **Phenolic bitterness** is scored on whites. **Tannin** is scored on reds.

read.bigIdea: Tie what’s in the glass to what you’ve studied.
read.where: Each wine in the Level 1 **Tasting Journal** ends with a **Wine Information Review**. You write down the wine tasted, then connect your notes to **theory**: grape, climate, place, quality level and **vintage**.

stops.name: Grape
stops.note: or the main one in a blend
stops.text: Name the grape. Then list **five** aromas and flavors that make this wine unique.

stops.name: Climate
stops.text: Choose **cool**, **moderate** or **warm**. Look at structure, mainly **acidity** and **alcohol**, to decide.

stops.name: Country, region, appellation
stops.text: Which **countries** classically grow this grape? Which **regions and appellations**?

stops.name: Quality level
stops.text: Use the region’s own levels. The journal lists **Burgundy**, **Beaujolais**, **Alsace**, **Rioja**, **Chianti** and **Germany**.

read.mixup: **Chianti Classico** is a place and quality level. **Sangiovese** is the grape.

sections.name: Climate and age in the glass

keyPoints.line: means tart fruit and more acidity.
means riper fruit, less acidity, more alcohol.

read.bigIdea: The glass can hint at climate and age.
read.where: The Court says to read climate from **fruit condition** and **structure**, mainly acidity and alcohol. Read age from fruit condition, color, fruit versus savory notes, and **sediment**.

stops.name: Cool climate
stops.text: Tart fruit and **higher acidity**. Cool reds tend to have **lower alcohol** and lighter body. Cool whites show citrus and green orchard fruit.

stops.name: Warm climate
stops.text: Riper fruit and **lower acidity**. Warm grapes build more sugar, so the wine has **more alcohol**.

stops.name: Age
stops.text: Fresh fruit turns more **dried** and concentrated as a wine develops. Whites move toward yellow and brown; reds fade and turn more transparent.

read.sayIt: It’s from a cool climate, so it’s crisp and bright.

video.title: Common Tasting Exam Mistake with David Keck, MS

keyPoints.line: is picked from six listed on the Certified exam.
is cool, moderate or warm.
from your notes back up every conclusion.
are 1-3, 4-6 or 7+ years on the Certified grid.
to a guest in two sentences or less.

read.bigIdea: Every answer needs a reason from your notes.
read.where: On the Certified grid you name the grape, climate, country and an age range. Give specific reasons from what you described. Then sell the wine to a guest in **two sentences or less**. At Level 1, the journal’s **Introduction to Deductive Tasting** pages make an **initial** conclusion (possible grapes, climate, possible countries, an age range of 1-3, 3-5, 5-10 or 10+ years), then a **final** one (grape, country, region and appellation, quality level, vintage).

stops.name: Grape
stops.text: Six grapes are listed on the exam, and the list changes from exam to exam.

stops.name: Climate
stops.text: Base it on **fruit condition** and **structure**.

stops.name: Country
stops.text: Name the **country of origin**.

stops.name: Check yourself
stops.text: If your notes say **off-dry** but you chose **Sauvignon Blanc**, look back for where things went off track.

read.mixup: The **Certified grid** asks for country. The **Advanced/Master** format adds region, appellation, quality level and vintage.

video.title: Chardonnay (everything you need to know) | Grapes 101

keyPoints.line: grows cool to warm; lees, malo and new oak are options.
is Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé; Fumé Blanc in California.
has high acidity and runs from dry to sweet.
is South Africa’s name for Chenin Blanc.

read.bigIdea: Four white grapes, each with its classic homes.
read.where: The Court’s **Grape Variety Profiles** show each grape’s **climates**, **top regions**, **styles**, **structure** and **color range**. Some region names **imply the grape**, and some grapes go by **other names**.

stops.name: Chardonnay
stops.text: Still or **sparkling**, and dry. It can be tart, fruity or decadent, oaked or unoaked. Possible steps: **lees contact**, **malolactic** and **new oak**. Top regions: **Burgundy**, **Champagne** (Blanc de Blancs), California, Oregon and Victoria.

stops.name: Sauvignon Blanc
stops.text: Dry or sweet, light to medium body, acidity toward high. Top regions: the **Loire** (**Sancerre**, **Pouilly-Fumé**), **Bordeaux** (Sauternes), **Marlborough**, Casablanca in Chile, and California, where it’s also **Fumé Blanc**.

stops.name: Riesling
stops.text: Dry, sweet or sparkling, with **high acidity** and light to medium body. Unoaked. Color runs from pale straw to deep gold. Top regions: **Southwest Germany**, **Alsace** and **Clare Valley** in Australia.

stops.name: Chenin Blanc
stops.text: Dry, sweet or sparkling, with acidity toward high. Top regions: the **Loire** (**Vouvray**, **Savennières**, **Bonnezeaux**, **Quarts de Chaume**) and **South Africa**, where it’s called **Steen**.

read.mixup: **Steen** is Chenin Blanc in South Africa. **Fumé Blanc** is Sauvignon Blanc in California.
read.sayIt: It’s a Riesling, so it’s bright and crisp, even when it’s a little sweet.

video.title: Pinot Noir (Everything you need to know) | Grapes 101

keyPoints.line: is Burgundy’s red; whole cluster is a possible step.
is marked high for both tannin and acidity.
is Syrah’s name in Australia (Barossa).
is Tuscany’s grape: Chianti and Brunello di Montalcino.
leads in Rioja, Ribera del Duero and Toro.

read.bigIdea: Eight red grapes, each with a classic home.
read.where: The red profiles add **tannin** to the structure bars. They also show each grape’s classic **bottle** and **glass**, and possible winemaking steps such as **blending**, **whole cluster** or **large barrels**.

stops.name: Pinot Noir
stops.text: Burgundy bottle and glass. Top regions: **Burgundy**, California, Oregon and **New Zealand**. Possible steps: **whole cluster**, neutral oak, new oak. Color: pale to deep ruby.

stops.name: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot
stops.text: Both use the **Bordeaux bottle**, with destemming, **blending** and new oak as possible steps. **Cabernet** grows moderate to hot (Bordeaux, California, Washington, Chile, Australia). **Merlot** grows moderate to warm (Bordeaux, California, Chile).

stops.name: Syrah and Grenache
stops.text: **Syrah** is **Shiraz** in Australia; its top regions are the **Northern Rhône** (Hermitage, Côte-Rôtie, Saint-Joseph) and **Barossa**. **Grenache** grows warm to hot in the **Southern Rhône**, Spain (**Garnacha Tinta**, **Garnatxa**) and Australia.

stops.name: Nebbiolo and Sangiovese
stops.text: **Nebbiolo** is marked **high** for tannin and acidity, and its color runs to garnet. It makes **Barolo** and **Barbaresco** in Piedmont, and **Valtellina** in Lombardy, where it’s called **Chiavennasca**. **Sangiovese** is Tuscany: **Chianti** and **Brunello di Montalcino**.

stops.name: Tempranillo
stops.text: Top regions: **Rioja**, **Ribera del Duero** (**Tinta del País**) and **Toro** (**Tinta de Toro**). Blending, large barrels, neutral oak and new oak are all possible steps.

read.mixup: **Barolo** and **Barbaresco** are Nebbiolo. **Chianti** and **Brunello** are Sangiovese.
read.sayIt: It’s Nebbiolo, so expect firm tannin and bright acidity.
